passages.quote: pH, dissolved oxygen, hydrogen, total gas content, conductivity, chlorides, fluorine, boron, and radioactivity.
The reason for controlling pH in the reactor coolant system is to minimize and control corrosion.
Control of the dissolved oxygen content in the reactor facility system is of paramount importance because of its contribution to increased corrosion.
Hydrogen gas (H2) and hydrazine (N2H4) are the scavenging agents normally used to eliminate dissolved oxygen from the reactor coolant system.
Total gas is the sum of all gases contained in the coolant system
Conductivity of reactor facility water is measured to provide an indication of dissolved ionic substances in the coolant.
Low conductivity is also an indicator of a potential problem because, in high purity basic systems, the only possible cause of low conductivity is a low pH.
the type of greatest concern is chloride stress corrosion.
First, F- promotes corrosion of zirconium by a stress corrosion mechanism at the inner surface of the clad
Radioactivity of the reactor coolant system is monitored and controlled because it is a good indicator of several conditions that may occur in the system.
When sufficient oxygen is added to deplete the hydrogen inventory, acidic pH results in those facilities where high (basic) pH is maintained.
If a defect were present or a failure of a fuel element occurred, large amounts of fission products would potentially have a path to the coolant system.
Another significant property of TMA is its intense odor of dead fish.
If overheating occurs, the ion exchanger should be taken out of service immediately and the cause rectified.

body.text: Radiation interacts with coolant water mainly by ionization.
In a closed system under pressure, H2 and O2 are confined, and an equilibrium state is reached.

checks.q: What is the overall effect of radiation on pure water?
checks.x: The net result of the reactions is simply the decomposition of water.

body.text: Normally, reactor coolant contains excess dissolved hydrogen, so there is no significant net decomposition of water by radiation.

checks.q: What is the advantage of maintaining excess hydrogen in reactor water?
o: It largely eliminates production of free oxygen
checks.x: The addition of H2 to reactor coolant largely eliminates production of free oxygen.

concepts.title: Air in the coolant: ammonia and nitric acid

body.text: After oxygen from air is consumed, hydrogen and nitrogen can remain.
If a large amount of air depletes the hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen form nitric acid.
One solution would be to add more hydrogen, which reacts with the remaining oxygen.

checks.q: What does excess oxygen and nitrogen form in reactor water?
checks.x: If oxygen remains after hydrogen is consumed, the oxygen-nitrogen reaction produces nitric acid.

checks.q: About how much nitrogen is converted to ammonia in reactor coolant?
checks.x: In most cases, less than about 10 percent of the nitrogen will be converted to ammonia.

body.text: Fast neutron and proton reactions with oxygen isotopes produce radioactive nitrogen and fluorine isotopes.

items: N-16 (7.13 second half-life) decays to O-16, with a high-energy gamma ray
N-17 (4.1 second half-life) decays to O-16, with a neutron and a gamma ray
N-13 (10 minute half-life) decays to C-13
F-18 (112 minute half-life) decays to O-18
Tritium (12.3 year half-life) forms from deuterium

body.text: N-16 and N-17 are carried outside the core and matter for shielding, but they decay quickly after shutdown.
From a few minutes to about five hours after shutdown, N-13 and F-18 are the principal sources of radioactivity in the coolant.

items: pH: inhibit corrosion and protect the corrosion film. Control by ion exchange and chemical addition
Dissolved oxygen: inhibit corrosion. Control by hydrogen or hydrazine addition
Hydrogen: scavenge oxygen and suppress radiolytic decomposition. Control by hydrogen addition and degassification
Total gas: protect pumps and indicate air in leakage. Control by degassification
Conductivity: minimize scale and indicate corrosion. Control by ion exchange, feed and bleed
Chlorides: preclude chloride stress corrosion. Control by ion exchange, feed and bleed
Fluorine: preclude corrosion of zirconium cladding. Control by ion exchange, feed and bleed
Boron: control reactivity. Control by boric acid addition
Radioactivity: indicate corrosion, crud bursts, fuel defects, and demineralizer performance

body.text: Hydrazine decomposes rapidly above about 200 °F, so hydrogen is used during hot operation.

checks.q: Why is hydrazine not used as an oxygen scavenger during hot operation?
checks.x: Because hydrazine decomposes rapidly above about 200 °F, hydrogen gas is used during hot operation.

checks.q: In a high purity basic system, what is the only possible cause of low conductivity?
checks.x: In high purity basic systems, the only possible cause of low conductivity is a low pH.

checks.q: Why is chloride kept at the minimum practicable level?
checks.x: The type of corrosion of greatest concern with chloride is chloride stress corrosion.

body.text: The reduced pH loosens the corrosion film, causing a crud burst, seen as increased radiation levels and conductivity and lower ion exchanger efficiency.
Gaseous radioactive levels would rise, and ion exchanger efficiency may fall because many fission products have lower affinity for the resin.
The anion resin begins to decompose slowly at about 140 °F.
Decomposition becomes rapid above 180 °F. The cation resin is stable up to about 250 °F.
Overheating can raise chlorides and radioactivity, reduce ion exchanger effectiveness, and change pH.

checks.q: What is an indication of resin overheating, though not definitive?
o: An intense odor of dead fish
checks.x: TMA has an intense odor of dead fish, which may give an indication of resin overheating.

checks.q: What should be done if resin overheats?
o: Take the ion exchanger out of service immediately
checks.x: If overheating occurs, the ion exchanger should be taken out of service immediately and the cause rectified.

facts.q: What are the nine reactor water chemistry parameters?
facts.a: pH, dissolved oxygen, hydrogen, total gas content, conductivity, chlorides, fluorine, boron, and radioactivity.

facts.q: What is the effect of adding excess hydrogen to reactor water?
facts.a: It forces the equilibrium toward water, so oxygen is consumed.

facts.q: Why is dissolved oxygen controlled in reactor water?
facts.a: Because of its contribution to increased corrosion.

facts.q: What does a fuel element failure do to the coolant?
facts.a: It gives large amounts of fission products a path to the coolant system.

summary.text: Radiation causes pure water to decompose into H2 and O2, and adding excess hydrogen suppresses it.
Very large air additions may produce more nitric acid than the basic coolant can neutralize.
Injection of air can deplete hydrogen and cause a pH swing, a crud burst, and higher radiation levels.
Resin overheating decomposes the resin, and its products affect coolant chemistry.

blend_notes.note: This topic is built under the Step 1 decision and tagged Water-system only on every page. It describes water reactor coolant throughout, so the later rule leaving out items tied to PWR or BWR coolant could not apply to all of it. Passages that name a PWR or BWR specifically are left off, including BWR oxygen, the pressurizer, and Figure 3.

Objective 1.4 asks for three sources of radioactivity, but the chapter gives N-16, N-17, N-13, F-18, and tritium, and does not name three. The lesson lists them all, and no check tests a count of three.
